chapters.title: Opening: 610,000 plays across ten episodes, and the website’s new transcript selection and export feature

Hi, everyone, I’m Orange.

chapters.title: GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol: criticism on X and confusion over review versions

paragraphs.value: The first thing I put on my list was the release of GPT-6.2, Astra and Sol. I felt like, that morning when I got up and looked at my whole Twitter feed, I thought, “What happened to this model? How did it get all these people so mad?” Everyone was trashing it. Those opinion leaders—every single opinion leader on Twitter was trashing it, and they were saying some really harsh things.

They were saying it was practically useless, a huge step backward. I tried it that morning and thought it was okay. Maybe it has something to do with how models are being released now. Everyone’s doing these myth-making, miracle-style launches, which keeps raising people’s expectations. If you don’t make some huge breakthrough, you might get… Before, if you didn’t make a huge breakthrough, nobody cared. But now, if you don’t make a huge breakthrough, people may just bash you.

I saw you looked into what people were saying about it afterward. Apparently Tibo himself said that the version they first gave KOLs to test wasn’t the same as the final release. He said that version really was bad, and the one they eventually released may have…
Fixed some things.
Fixed some things.
But I think this…
Let me add something.

chapters.title: Sol Ultra Fast feels fast and economical; Astra is expensive, struggles with frontend design, and argues

paragraphs.value: I actually tried it, and the model that pleasantly surprised me most was the Ultra Fast model in 6.2 Sol. Wow, that one is really fast. It can do things both quickly and reliably. That’s the only pleasant surprise, I think. But Ultra (Astra) still feels expensive as ever, and the quality isn’t good. Especially when I ask it to make a webpage, its frontend design sense is still terrible.
You mean Ultra Fast is really good, but Ultra isn’t, right?
Astra—I mean 6.2.
Oh, Astra.
The 6.2 Sol one, the ultra-fast mode.
Yeah.

He said Ultra Fast really is good. And what’s best about Ultra Fast? It doesn’t burn through your usage allowance as much. If you’re on the $200 plan, it won’t eat through your allowance that badly. It really is fast and good. But compared with… I tested it that day by having it edit a video. Maybe my editing was pretty fragmented, the video-editing task was pretty fragmented, but it peaked at nearly 300 tokens per second—260, maybe 270.

From our perspective, especially after Codex has been giving us such a hard time with rate limits for over a month—we’ve been dealing with that for over a month—it feels really fast. But then you think about it, and it still isn’t as fast as DeepSeek.
That’s true.
Yeah, DeepSeek has gotten faster recently after blocking a lot of web users on the consumer side, and people have had some pretty mixed reactions.
__, speaking of DeepSeek.

Let’s not get sidetracked. So, about Sol: they said they started beta testing with KOLs two weeks ago, and it was really bad then. They gave a lot of feedback, and the company changed a whole bunch of things. But… But that KOL said there were still problems after the changes. He thought the problem was that the model was kind of hard to understand. It did the work okay—that was generally agreed, like making 3D stuff and doing some common-sense tasks were fine—but you couldn’t make sense of its feedback.
It stopped talking like a normal person.

There were mainly three problems, I think. One was that it got much worse at talking like a normal person, almost to the level of Opus 4.7, 4.8. The second thing? It still had its old problem: being overly defensive. Oh, right—wasn’t there a meme yesterday? Someone said good morning to Gemini, and Gemini said, “Hi, the weather’s nice today.”

Then Claude (Astra) also said hi and offered some kind of well-wish. Claude (Astra) said, “Just to clarify, today…” He said the weather was nice and sunny. Then Claude (Astra)—no, Astra—said, “Just bear in mind that it might not be sunny,” and so on.
It kept arguing back against the statement that it was sunny today.
__, this…
It completely missed the “good morning” part.
That’s my nightmare, you know? Lately, chatting with DeepSeek has been like that too. Whatever you say, it has to argue with you. It’s just like the comments section on X, you know?
It really can be overly defensive. It always assumes you’re trying to get around it or trick it into something.
It just has to play devil’s advocate. It’s so annoying.

I'm flattered.

chapters.title: Why evaluation is getting harder as expectations rise and everyday coding approaches saturation

paragraphs.value: What I mainly wanted to talk about is the evaluation side of things.
You mean the AA one?

No, I mean the overseas KOLs being sent models to test. The promotion around models being sent out for testing—I think lately it’s not just OpenAI that’s had this problem. A lot of our domestic models have run into it too. When they promote them, there may be a disconnect: they themselves think the models are really good.
Yeah.
I'm sure OpenAI itself thought it was OK; that's why they released it. If they knew this was how it would turn out, they definitely wouldn't have released it. They're not crazy, right?

They set the benchmark really high, and then the experience creates a huge contrast and disconnect for everyone, which can easily lead to... whether ordinary users or KOLs... Especially with OpenAI, they tell me, “Say whatever you want,” right? So I just speak plainly, and that’s not OK. And overseas opinion leaders or KOLs, wherever they’re from, all have an incentive to get traffic.
If you tell me I can say whatever I want, then of course I'm going to say something more outrageous, because that way I'll get more traffic.
Right.
I think models have raised everyone's expectations too high now.
Yeah.
If this version doesn't show me anything impressive that I can brag about, I'll give it a bad review.
Maybe that's a KOL problem. They're also getting to the point where they can't find much to test, so everyone looks for something to get emotional about.
I think that's a really good point you made. They're getting to the point where they can't find much to test. This may be a general pattern for new models released from here on.
And you can't really... If you give me a model now and ask me to evaluate it within a week, I don't think I can. A lot of the time, I just can't.
Yeah.

Because they’re all pretty similar. But that kind of vibe coding, where you say one sentence and something comes out—that’s become completely useless, because when you see the result, you realize you can no longer evaluate whether it’s good or bad.
Or maybe we could put it another way: they've more or less absorbed software and the internet and all that.
It's over.
Look at the new directions now, including what Anthropic talked about around its IPO. What was it? Biology.
Healthcare.

Healthcare—solving people’s health problems. And earlier, they released something about law and things like that. They’ve already started moving into fields including embodied AI, right? The various fields of science. For us everyday, so-called internet people, if we want it to make a game, create 3D content, or build a product, we’re pretty much at the end of the road in the digital world.
Yeah, Fable too. Its intelligence score didn’t improve, and its coding score didn’t improve either.
But when you chat with Fable, you have to talk to it more to feel that kind of...
Intelligence.
Real intelligence. That kind of foresight, that quality of a leader.
Right.
And then pulling together all that breadth of knowledge, connecting it all, and giving you a conclusion that feels really convincing.
Yeah.
That kind of feeling.

Is it because people can't really distinguish the models on coding anymore, so they've started paying attention to other details, like flashes of inspiration, or precision in how it expresses itself, or how pleasant it is to interact with? Are those areas where the shortcomings are starting to show, and people are slowly trying to make them up?
But these things are all really subtle, you know?
Yeah. Because coding is very objective, and by now it's basically reached all programmers. If there are still programmers who aren't using AI, right? They might not really be keeping up.
Fine, no need to use it.
Yeah, look at Anthropic after Opus 5.5 came out. Its revenue and usage actually didn't increase, which means it's already saturated.
Right. So why does everyone think Google is good? Because Google was so bad before.
Mm-hmm.
You need to have that—you need to create that contrast.
Right.
Right. It wasn't intentional, either.
Yeah. Next, OpenAI's next model: as long as it's not really bad, people are sure to rate it well. Why? There isn't anything worse left.
Because 6.2 was so bad.
Yeah, mainly because they held out for two and a half months.

Regression to the mean, right? It's like that psychological effect. You do badly on a test, your parents scold you, and then you do well on the next one. But it wasn't because you got scolded; it's just regression to the mean.
Yeah.
Hey, you have to admit, Company A picked a really good time to go public.
Yeah.
Yeah, at this point it's the strongest, way out in front.
Way out in front, for sure.

chapters.title: Two approaches to 3D: Fable 5.2’s atmosphere versus Astra’s detailed Blender modeling

paragraphs.value: Next, I tried Astra. Its 3D improvements are really lopsided, but the part it’s focused on is really good. A lot of people say Fable is good at modeling, but it does that through Three.js, frontend effects, and being ahead on the coding side.

It's really good at creating atmosphere. It doesn't actually do that well at the fundamentals of modeling, like sculpting model details, materials, and textures. Its details aren't good. So what is it good at? The whole scene has a sense of beauty. It combines all kinds of random little things—not very finely detailed things—into a really beautiful scene, then adds things like volumetric fog and rendering to make the whole scene look beautiful. That's how it does it.

Astra is really good at modeling. Instead of giving it a scene, give it a strong central subject and it can do an excellent job. It uses Blender, generates its own textures, and finds additional textures to build the scene. Especially for irregular shapes—not the boxy kind that can be made with bpy. We’re not talking about modeling with bpy; Python. It uses line drawing and mathematics to model them.

Why do so many people build cities? Because city buildings are all rectangular blocks. That's easy. As soon as you give it something like an old Chinese building or something in a forest that needs sculpting, it can't do it. But Astra—look, the other day I gave it this really crooked, twisted pine tree.
A dragon, right?

A pine tree—a really twisted pine tree with a Chinese building on it. A very complex Chinese building. The picture was a reference image; it was generated, and not a single part matched the original. So it had to build the structure piece by piece, sculpt the pine tree, and find new textures to fit the original reference image. In the end, it was perfect from every angle, even though the picture only showed one view.
In the end, what it generated could be rotated all the way around, and it had all the volumetric stuff it needed, all the snow and everything. A different approach.
I'm curious. If they're all competing in this kind of 3D, what kind of huge impact could that have on traditional 3D modeling companies?

I think there are two cases. With something like Opus 5.5, the way it competes in 3D is by building aesthetic scenes. It also competes on coding and things like that. It doesn't compete on modeling details; it doesn't go after that. Maybe it figures the returns are low, so it hasn't added that kind of training data. That could be an advantage for 3D modeling companies.

Because it needs to rely on tools from 3D modeling companies to do that detailed sculptural modeling. But if you look at OpenAI continuing to push into fundamental, realistic modeling—the kind of model you're actually supposed to build, meaning modeling a single subject—I think that's a bad sign for 3D modeling companies.
I feel like OpenAI specifically added this data. They added a lot of data, so it became lopsided. Anthropic seems to have some generalization; it actually hasn't been particularly...
Right.

...focused on it. There's also a rumor that this time Astra will add some robotics data. But it seems no one's tested it yet. Last time, they also saw the robotics data generalizing, and then they strengthened it further. It should be even stronger this time.

Orange put that really well. You know, when we talked about Fable last episode, a lot of the way Fable expressed things was through brushstrokes. It was like a person painting, adding it one stroke at a time, then revealing the picture at the very end, and you think it's perfect. And there's lighting and shadows in it. I think that still comes down to how it describes things, its understanding of aesthetics or of the information.
It's not specifically about 3D modeling.

It’s like Fable has a model of beauty in its brain. I gave Fable and Sol the same prompt and asked Sol to make something in the most beautiful way, and the result was awful. I played the skiing game Fable made. That game was really great. There was someone skiing, and when I tried it with Astra and Sol, they were just like—we’d call them blocks—a bunch of blocks.
Minecraft, right?
Minecraft, skiing.
Turn it into Minecraft.
The gameplay is pretty decent, but the feel of it is nowhere near Opus or Fable.
I feel like with OpenAI's...
Could they fix it just by adding more data?
Huh?
Could it fill in the data and solve this part? For a company like OpenAI, for example.
I think so, I guess...
I don't know.

But that's a huge amount of data. Adding more now, or using old data, definitely won't work. What I was going to say just now is, I think OpenAI's infrastructure team has a big problem. They have no taste. Taste is really important now.

Didn't we say last time that Fable has an aesthetic sense, and in some ways it's even surpassed people? But OpenAI's stuff looks really shoddy. You do web development, right? You said the webpages it makes are hideous.
Wow, I looked and there it was again: pale green. You can tell at a glance it's the standard GPT color scheme. There's just no second style at all.
It's just like what I was talking about earlier—the feel of Opus, Astra, and Neon is very similar. They're all the same.
Right.
Language and wording, and then aesthetics—those are really all part of the same thing.
Right. Taste is all connected. Neon is, well...

chapters.title: Carbon and Neon make writing feel human again

paragraphs.value: For example, Orange experiences it mainly through language and text, and from the perspective of agents—especially Cola Agent.

Because it’s much closer to our users’ use cases. Our users aren’t programmers. We don’t have programmers here; they’re mostly people doing personal projects on their own, or using it for work, and there’s a lot of writing too. And in writing, it’s clearly way ahead. This industry hasn’t had a model that’s good at writing for a whole year.

Carbon is way ahead. Didn’t I already hype it up last week? But I’m keeping it up this week. You know how good it is? The biggest writing software company in China certified it as the best model. __. It’s wild. In the online fiction world right now, it has no competition.
Really?
Last time—last time we talked about Opus 4.6. That was a year ago.
Right, and AI detectors can’t tell that something was written by Carbon.
__. __, this is great news.

It’s the same with Neon. Someone tested it and said they had Neon organize something for them and write an article. They couldn’t find a single thing wrong with it. Didn’t need to edit anything; it didn’t feel AI-written. It’s terrifying.

I think it’s less about an AI feel. “It’s not this, but that”—I think that’s overused, some formulaic expression being overused. If you say, “It’s not this, but that,” well, normal people say that too. But it doesn’t feel awkward when he does it. Why? Because his “not this, but that” belongs right there.
Right.
More often, the issue isn’t that it sounds like AI; it’s whether you’ve used the right expression in the right place.
Right.

Let me give you an analogy. In terms of written expression, how should I put it… a sense of space. The Neon I’ve been using, right? Compared with Astra, it feels like the distance between a three-dimensional being and a two-dimensional being. One is especially flat; the other can use words you’d never imagine. Right, let me read you something. This is how I tested it. I’m still working on that big Bilink project of mine.

Right.
I was touched right away.
Right.
All right.

chapters.title: Native multimodality: understanding and recreating fast animation, with design taste beyond Opus 5.5

paragraphs.value: I think Neon has good aesthetic taste. You were just talking about the copy, right? In terms of aesthetic taste, it has a sense of design, and some of that spatial quality you mentioned in multimodal work. You see it in the design too. Overall, speaking just about aesthetics… maybe it’s still a little behind Opus on engineering. I don’t think it’s much behind, but maybe it falls a little short on long tasks.
In aesthetics and taste, whatever kind of taste it is, whether it’s design, front-end, or literature, it’s stronger than Opus 5.5. In anything involving taste, it’s stronger than Opus 5.5.
Then it’s not as strong as Fable.
Fable has a different kind of taste—more high-dimensional, more forward-looking, more like a sage. It shows in its performance, rather than in its aesthetic qualities.
Okay.
Right.
So it’s number one in aesthetics now.
I think so. And what’s one issue with it?
It’s very highly rated.

It’s natively multimodal. When you ask Claude to look at an animation and recreate it—no, when you ask Claude to look at an animation and recreate it, you find that it actually can’t see the animation. You have to describe in words how something moves from here to there, from here to there. It can only infer the animation by comparing the frames before and after.

But Neon really understands how this thing is supposed to move, so when it comes to making animations, Neon is stronger than Opus 5.5. And when it’s referencing an animation, during some of the rapid changes, the faster the changes, the better the result.

Agreed, because traditional multimodal models aren’t truly native. What Guizang just said about it being native—I think that’s still really important. Otherwise, if you can only capture the frames before and after like this, you’re definitely going to miss details.

chapters.title: DeepMind’s turnaround: printed criticism and Sergey Brin’s return

paragraphs.value: Right.

Another thing I’m really curious about: Google hadn’t released a model in a long time, and now it has. At the same time, it’s also made organizational changes. For example, the legendary Jeff Dean and others have left. I’m curious what exactly changed inside the organization that allowed it to put out so many excellent models so quickly and so densely.
I’m pretty curious about this part. I wonder if anyone knows.
I reposted something about this this morning. They—their official account—whose phone keeps going off?
Mine.

Someone from their official team posted this morning, saying they were especially grateful to—what was it called? Uh, SemiAnalysis. They published an article in August criticizing DeepMind, saying all their researchers had left, their models were terrible, the lab was finished, and that the odds of them becoming SOTA again were zero.

Their team printed out the article and stuck it on their desks. They left it there for months to remind themselves every day. From that angle, I think they realized they had problems before, and they really did manage to bring the team together. Google certainly doesn’t lack data or chips. It was still a people problem. They’ve solved that people problem now.

I think founder Sergey Brin is really important. With a founder and without a founder, it’s completely… A founder running things and a founder not running things really makes for two completely different companies.
Right.

Look, I don’t think Sundar could have pulled off this kind of integration. He just doesn’t have that—look at what he’s done before and you can tell he doesn’t have that ability. He couldn’t manage DeepMind and Hassabis, right? So it had to be Sergey Brin who did it. Now think about it: ByteDance and Google are really similar.

Before—we haven’t talked about this on the show, but didn’t I tell you guys privately? With ByteDance and Google alike, there’s absolutely no problem with talent density, and there’s absolutely no problem with computing resources. What needs to happen is for one person to lead, someone with the influence to bring everyone together and get something done.

Before, everyone was just doing their own thing. Every part was doing its own thing, and every part was excellent. But the problem is, when you’re working on something as cutting-edge as large models today, you need to bring everyone together. People have even said that they released several models this time. One explanation is that these models were developed in a race against each other.

That works too. You can bring each team together, and if you have enough resources for four or five teams racing against each other, that’s like having four or five NeoLabs. They can all go build something.
As long as they don’t go off doing all that other stuff—working on weather models today, and whatever else tomorrow…
World models and stuff.
They’ve made pretty good progress on world models too.
Oh, right.
They released one too. Genie 4, right?

Right, Genie 4. And what’s even more impressive is how abundant their computing resources are. Everyone else’s world models are just for showing off. For an internal preview, you probably only get a few days to test it, with access for around ten people. They released the Genie 4 API.
Oh, __, it’s available for commercial use. That’s pretty impressive.
That’s wild.
Actually, look at how enormous their computing resources are. Training a model over 12T is something I can’t even imagine, and Carbon has been live for so many days.

Insane.

And they’re doing it in parallel. If the overall compute, architecture, and data were the same, I don’t think they’d need to do that. So these two models are completely different, with completely different post-training approaches.
They’re going in different directions.
Maybe even the data is different. This is a pretty substantial task.
They’re not quite the same. Argon is a little better at writing. But it’s already been taken down from the official site; you can only access it through the API now.

chapters.title: Why Chinese Models Struggle to Grow Token Usage: High-Value Users Buy Top-Tier Overseas Models, While Users Just Trying to Get the Job Done Take Advantage of Free Access

paragraphs.value: I was talking with a friend in the industry this week about this problem with token usage on Chinese models. It just can't seem to go up, no matter what. I said the reason is simple: people who really use these models will pay for the best overseas models. What do the people who don't know much do? They make a list of where they can get tokens for free from Chinese products.

I can show you how to get free stuff from Doubao, and those people will all go use that. The people who pay just go straight to the best paid option, right? People who don't want to spend money just go straight for the free stuff.
There are two groups among so-called office workers. The first group really cares about output, about code quality. They work for themselves.
They'll find a way to use the best.
They work for themselves, so at that point they have to think about ROI.
Right.
They have to think about their time and money. They really can make money from this.
Right.

They have to consider all that, so they'll find a way to use the best model. Like with Anthropic banning accounts this time, right? A lot of people say, 'I can't use Anthropic, so I'll use Devin or something else.' Even if it's something else, I'll just treat it as that...
Five times as expensive.
Five times as expensive, and I'll just treat the extra money I'm spending as my...
Efficiency gains.

Efficiency gains. It saves me time, so I don't have to play these games with it anymore. That's fine. But what's the other kind? The other kind of work—'work' in quotation marks—is where I'm just checking a box. As long as I can produce something, it doesn't matter if it's good or bad. It has nothing to do with me.
Right.
It's just a job. You just have to put in eight hours.
The boss isn’t going to give me money to buy a better model. I’ll use whatever’s free and just turn in the work. So there are two groups of office workers.
Right.

The first group might be pretty small, but they generate a lot of value because they're really making money with this. They're willing to put money into it. No matter how expensive you are, if your model is good, they'll accept paying a bit more. But I don't think the second group adds much value.

Right, the data from that second group is low-value, too. For example, WorkBuddy announced about 10 million daily active users. Suppose 7 million of them go every day to claim a food delivery coupon and then stop using it. What value does that data have? It has no value.
Absolutely no loyalty.
Loyalty, too—this data is garbage; repetitive tasks like these are no use to new models.

To put it bluntly, those people are actually less valuable than the people playing 'Big Fat Fish' on DeepSeek Harness—the people raising fish. Raising fish can even improve their language expression, their emotions...
That data is useful.

Right, it becomes richer, and the companionship gets better. People also get to experience some variety and different ways to play. They’re willing to spend time on the fish-raising feature, too. As for office work, I think these are the two groups we have right now. We can’t serve the very top tier of users. Our models just can’t serve that very top tier.
So from this angle, the quality of the training data can’t improve.
The data flywheel hasn't gotten going. But it looks like Zhipu is about to release a new model. Before, Zhipu had been pretty focused on...
Everyone’s really looking forward to that recent Anthropic one. This big KYC wave? People have actually been saying, “When are the domestic models going to release another large model?”
Actually... but I'm still pretty excited, because last time... that one was probably the one Qwen released recently. People were still a bit disappointed.

chapters.title: Advice for model launches: show a complete real project instead of claiming to beat Opus 5.5

paragraphs.value: I think this is a marketing problem with how we launch Chinese models. I think we need to...
Be more practical. More practical. Stop saying every time that you're going to beat Opus 5.5.

I think you need to believe what you say yourselves, at the very least. You say you can beat Claude Opus 5.5—do you believe that yourselves? Let me put it this way: ask the training researchers or people in charge at every Chinese model company to sit here, and ask them, “Can you really beat Claude Opus 5.5?”
No one dares say, “I can really beat Opus 5.5.” Even OpenAI can’t. What makes you think you can? What makes you the one?
If he dares, let him stand right here and record a video saying it. Do you dare? No one has the guts to stand up and say, “I’m better than Opus 5.5.” No one dares say that.
No, no. People call it a more affordable alternative, or say it’s close—that’s the kind of language that frames it as a follower.
I think it’s an implication—implying that I’m in the same league as Opus 5.5.
Right, right, right.

But I think we need to get rid of this kind of caricatured, slogan-driven promotion. Just tell people the truth: users aren’t stupid, especially people in the field. You need to tell them about your model. First, you need to understand your own model. I’ve genuinely made progress in certain areas, I think.

What are some good cases we’ve run? But why? How are people supposed to use it? Look at the kinds of articles Anthropic keeps putting out: they keep explaining how they build their harness. They don’t keep talking about the model, but they go all out promoting how to use it.
How should you use this model? My harness, my agent, including my… Personal Agent—how they’re built. They’ve been quite open about all of this, I think, except for not open-sourcing it.
How to push cache utilization to the limit—that’s the kind of thing they talk about.

And a lot of the time, what I’ve noticed is this: look at all the evaluations and promotional materials we do here in China. Even the brief will say, “Make a few really fancy things.” But lately I’ve been liking that approach less and less. Ideally, you take a real project you’re working on and run it with the model, showing the whole process.
Right.
It might not look so fancy to the general public, and there may not be many examples, but that really makes for a better case. It can clearly explain the model’s strengths and weaknesses.
Or, when people ask for fancy things, they don’t know what fancy means. They have no idea what the fanciest thing their own model can make is.

I understand that you want a good case study, or that you need people who are good at using models to come up with one. But what I think you should do is talk with them and have them help you understand where your model is strong. First, you need to be able to produce good case studies. Look at Anthropic or OpenAI: every time they launch something, they have lots of examples.

They can do a really good job themselves. Of course, we have examples too—we do. Where are ours? Problems caused by copying keep coming up. I think we need to avoid that and focus much, much more on evaluations, or model evaluations.
Okay.
Okay, let’s keep going.
Because the audience for this segment is too small right now. There are only 10 of us altogether.
Maybe 100 people across all of China at most. Let’s leave it at that.
People have also recently been using Neon for 3D and image generation. They’ve been asking it to draw, as they do with Opus 5.5 or Fable 5.2, and the results are pretty good.
Pretty good, too.
Neon’s style is actually pretty different from Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.2. It’s good in a different way.
It just has its own thing going on.
Right.
It has its own aesthetic logic because it hasn’t been distilled.
Right. And it’s really good, too. That’s pretty important. Diversity is pretty important.
This is great. Suddenly, today, the world has become a diverse place.
Right.
Instead of everyone having to watch Anthropic keep shutting us out.

chapters.title: Building video graphics and automatic podcast highlights with Neon

Yesterday I used Neon. Before I went out to eat, I gave it a prompt. I wanted to add a feature to my podcast app that automatically cuts highlight clips. It was really simple, just two or three sentences of prompting. When I got back, holy crap, I was shocked. It was incredibly complete, and it fit in so well with my existing features.

For example, the existing feature is a podcast with Chinese and English subtitles on the right. It designed an entry point called “Highlights” above the subtitles. When I click it, it automatically calls an AI model and turns all the moments it thinks are interesting into individual cards. I just have to click one clip, and it opens this page where I can preview it, see the cover, export it directly, and precisely trim that segment.
So I thought, holy crap, this can absolutely be a stand-in for Claude Opus 5.5—and it’s a really, really clever design.
Right.
It has this kind of… product design capability built in. It’s not just executing tasks.

chapters.title: A True Million-Token Needle-in-a-Haystack Test and a Ten-Thousand-Character Article Generated in One Pass

paragraphs.value: It benefits from its real context capabilities. And what else does Google have? Google's context window is really powerful. That one million is a real one million; it doesn't shrink in the middle. A lot of models do needle-in-a-haystack tests, and they fall apart once you get to the middle. Google's is really strong. It stays above 70% the whole time, which means when it looks at your code—not a very long codebase, that is—

It can examine things in great detail. It can really read all your interaction design plans and your design plans, as well as some of the interaction logic you’ve used before. It can reuse that, which is great. And I think in some respects it’s even better than Opus 5.5. Why? They each have their strengths, and once its particular strengths fill in the gaps, it’s a model in the same league as Opus 5.5.

chapters.title: Strong model, frustrating tools: Antigravity’s weak caching and clumsy permissions, and the Windsurf team’s need for faster feedback-driven iteration

paragraphs.value: What do I think is the worst part right now? Its model is great, but its Harness just doesn't measure up to the model. Its Harness is from the previous generation.
Right.

What it urgently needs now, like Pan said, is to iterate faster and get up to the general standard for Harnesses today. For example, its product manager listed several pieces of feedback from people yesterday. The first one: their caching isn't good enough; it tops out at 85%. But look at DeepSeek and lots of other models—their cache hit rates are 95%, 98% or higher.

Second, Orange complained about this before too: its permission controls are really dumb. You give it automatic permissions, and it still keeps popping up prompts. So it clearly hasn't gotten these little features right. And as we just said, things like context management, control, and compression—its context window is long, but it still needs compression. It's really fallen short on all of that.
So I think this team also needs what I was just talking about… It's gotten feedback from a lot of users, so now it has a data-driven iteration flywheel.
Exactly.
I believe Google should catch up pretty quickly, because AI coding tools are moving really fast right now, right?

Just dumped them; it didn't use any tools at all, just output them directly.

Right, edits it. Right. Right.
It's the one that does the massive output in a single blast.
It ran for a whole hour to write a novel. The kind where it spits out ten thousand characters.

Look, the key people on the Antigravity team used to be at Windsurf. Right? They made Windsurf, and Windsurf was pretty good back then. Then they joined Google and it turned into this. Look how chaotic it is.

I think for this team, too, there's no strong positive feedback. Like, look at us: we've been doing our podcast lately, right? We keep getting positive feedback, so we keep iterating. They don't have a good model, so there's nowhere for that positive feedback to come from.
And then you won't let me use other models.
This thing is exactly like Doubao.

Right?
It's good. Because it also comes with subsidies, and the subsidies are pretty generous, so it's quite a good deal.

Instinct.

The person in charge at Muse went on a podcast and talked about what they originally thought the use cases for Muse would be and so on, but then they found that after launch, the biggest demand was shopping. In other words, having an agent shop for you. Overseas, this is a complete case of overtaking on a bend, like we said last time.
Now, shopping on their website is handled by agents.
Because Amazon is more like JD.com.
Right.
Amazon's range of items... the variety of products is...

Really inadequate. It's only good for big-ticket and very industrialized products. Like, some of the electronics and other common categories you often see on JD.com—each category might only have twenty or thirty of the better-selling items. But if you want to hunt for something really out there, or something you need that you can't find, you can only go to Shopify or some independently run overseas shopping sites, those websites, to get it.
Before, you just couldn't find it there.
Couldn't find it.

They go looking on Amazon, and what problem do they often run into? They search Amazon for some little thing, and there's really nothing usable, and what they do find is super expensive, right? Then they can only search around on websites, but they don't have any good reputation, or go through some other route—and they don't dare buy it. That's what Muse does. And Shopify is completely open.
Do you think Shopify will get acquired by someone down the line?
Old Ma.
Its ecosystem is really good, because Amazon has even blocked agents. Right, Shopify is fully supportive.
Embracing them—fully embracing them.
And they're all independent sites. Think about it: this ecosystem does the best job of serving consumers.
Right.
Yeah.
And that CEO—their CEO's understanding of agents and AI, I think, is really on point.
Very, very, very aggressive.

chapters.title: Agents creating purchasing demand: digital pianos, lactase, and overseas supplements

paragraphs.value: And agent shopping actually makes a lot of sense. Even in China, where we can't have it shop directly for us, we recently bought an electric piano for our family.
An electric piano.

We gave our Cola the three models we were considering and asked her to research them. She recommended one, saying it was the best value for money and that if we didn't need that feature, we should get this one. So that's the one we bought. Wow, this research is...
So where did it get its data?
From searching.
But here in China, isn't it online...
They sell it overseas too.
That piano model—we had to buy an imported one, and people had shared their opinions on them. It could also look at social media and find some of that. It has its own sources.
Right.
Like we said last time, DeepSeek is really good at searching.
For example, SMZDM.
Just think, this is much more efficient than scrolling through Xiaohongshu yourself and having to look at a bunch of ads.

And Personal Agents can create shopping demand. They can create real shopping demand. I might need something this week—when you're scrolling up and down, the things it pushes at you don't interest you at all. It annoys the hell out of you every day; you're like, why do you keep showing me ads? See, it's because you don't have that need. Right now, you don't—right now you don't need this thing. And when you really do need it, it stops showing it to you, because it doesn't know when you'll need it.

For example, I've been using Muse lately. I've gone back to Muse—why? Grok Bot really hasn't been working very well. Yesterday I asked it to print today's draft—“thunderous mega-print”—and it printed out 15 pages of draft. It was completely unreadable. I couldn't stop it; it just started printing. When I was using Muse, I started out chatting about that Anthropic article on agents. Halfway through, I said, I've been having an upset stomach a lot lately, when I drink milk...

Because I'm lactose intolerant too, and I always thought lactose intolerance was incurable, that there was no treatment. It told me I could buy lactase, that there's oral lactase. I had no idea that existed. After I started taking lactase, I didn't have to drink lactose-free milk anymore; I could drink regular milk. I just have to take some lactase before drinking milk or having dairy.
I had no idea about that kind of need... If you're just scrolling up and down, that kind of recommendation model could never recommend it to me.
It can't recommend it; it doesn't have your context.

It also didn't know I was lactose intolerant. So I looked it up and bought it, and it's been really useful. There are lots of things you can't figure out how to use, or that you feel don't work well; more often, I think, the information just isn't conveyed well. For example, with supplements we buy, a lot of the time they arrive from overseas with everything in English. I have no idea, and the rules say you can't have all these random stickers on them. I have no idea how much I'm supposed to take or what they're even for.

Once you've bought them, you just tell it, and it'll... teach you how to take them. It'll also look things up to help you take them. Supplements aren't a big deal; they're not medicine, so it doesn't matter if it gets something wrong. I told it, I have that health record in Muse, you know, and I can pull in my Apple Watch data and my weekly strength-training data.

I said, I don't think this health record is quite enough. I said, if I tell you I'm sick, write it down for me, and keep track of the supplements I'm taking now too, including some of my health issues and things like that. Check in on me regularly, and then that brings about even more shopping demand.

chapters.title: Privacy and the trust flywheel: useful results encourage users to share health data and browser access

paragraphs.value: Look at the old products: they were constantly stealing your privacy, trying all sorts of things, listening in and stuff...
Now you're giving it to them yourself.
Now you're contributing it to them yourself, because you get a better experience. Before, they couldn't give you a better experience.

I met AJ in Hong Kong—I met AJ in Hong Kong yesterday—and AJ showed me his phone. He really sends everything to his Personal Agent, Instinct. It's all in there. If it can help people solve their problems, people are willing to give up all kinds of privacy. Bank cards and everything, no problem.
This week, JPMorgan and others all got attacked, and a bunch of user data was leaked.
Several banks and these financial underwriters for securities were attacked.
Right, but the people targeted had assets worth more than 10 million.
So everyone says, “It’s got nothing to do with me. It’s not my problem.”

There’s also Muse. It’s been putting out some pretty big updates lately, and its Spaces are really good. What else is good about Muse? It launched a browser extension. The Muse browser extension is connected to Muse itself. When you open a chat in the extension, all your context from Muse loads into it, so you can have it control the browser from there. It’s this experience where everything is connected across all channels.
Wherever you open it, it has all your context.
That’s good.

That’s what makes browser extensions useful. Nobody’s making browser extensions anymore, but Muse’s browser extension is useful, and it has browser use built in. It can read the browser and help you fill things out. You know how you wouldn’t let me… use Amazon? Then I’ll just use its browser extension, and use the browser to help me shop. And it works really well.

Yeah, because shopping is their biggest use case, so they’re bound to optimize for it. And the best way to do that is with a browser extension. It’s like when Xie Yang first worked on turning podcasts into text: browser extensions are unbeatable. You can just click once and do all sorts of things.
It just pulled it right down.
So there are some real heavy hitters on the Muse product team. They’re really good.
They really are. I think a lot of the time it really does...

This also makes me think of something Orange said before. How should I put it? Once you get something going and start getting positive feedback, you can build on it quickly. If you can’t get positive feedback, you drop it, and it stops being useful.

Actually, one thing about that positive feedback is that a Personal Agent is fundamentally about trust. Once you trust it, you give it more and more of your data. Then you get more help from it. That’s the first positive feedback loop. But if you don’t trust it—say the model is bad at first, the quality is poor, and you think it’s kind of stupid—you won’t give it information.
You won’t give it context.
Going back to the UI issue we talked about before: look, Muse and Grok Bot keep updating. They put out tons of updates every day, but the interface doesn’t change at all.
Right.
It doesn’t change at all. A friend told me yesterday that the Gemini app can connect to iMessage. It turns into something like a Personal Agent.
Oh.
You can talk to it and chat with it right there in iMessage, and it can also do scheduled tasks and all sorts of things.
So that means it’s online in the cloud too.
It’s already online in the cloud.

chapters.title: Apple’s personal-agent plans beyond Siri, and the case for cloud models

They’ve already greenlit the project.
The Siri era is finally coming to an end. I’m so happy.
Siri’s over again? Siri already died once.
No, this project is already over.

Remember how everyone used to say, “Oh, local models, local agents,” right? When the Mac mini was selling well, everyone was hyping it up, saying, “I’m going to get off the cloud and go back to local privacy.” I’m telling you, in the end, everyone has to go back to the cloud.

Nobody’s doing that stuff. The other night I was talking with Wenjun. Someone asked, “Does everyone need some kind of cross-agent context system? I built my own.” I said, “No. Most people don’t need that. Just give everything to whichever one works best, and that’s it.” That’s everyone. Those are the target users for Personal Agents.
It’s not about its value; it’s about the kind of person they are. They don’t have time to mess around with this stuff, and they don’t want to either.
Right.
I care about solving my problem. What do I care what server the person I’m talking to is on?

chapters.title: Smart-home assumptions and Ant’s different approaches with Lingguang and Afu

paragraphs.value: But things are strange in China, you know? What are they pushing here? Whether it’s Lingguang or whoever, they’re pushing Personal Agents to control home devices. It’s really strange. Think about it: how many people have smart-home devices? And what’s so fun about controlling them?
To put it bluntly, and this thing...

It’s all people in ivory towers making things for themselves.

And look, Afu has a pretty good reputation. But I think Afu is too narrowly focused. You can offer that, but you can’t position your whole value around health, because then I won’t open you unless I have a health problem.
What it really needs is an idea like, well...
A companion for everyday life.
No, there’s that book of his, called something like Live to 100, or Beyond 100. The idea is that being truly healthy means you don’t go to the hospital.
Your lifestyle.
Change your lifestyle and extend your...
Healthy lifespan.
Healthy lifespan, not lifespan. That’s the goal.
Like recommending some lactase.

You’re a little low on lactase. Today’s your strength-training day, right? You’re clearly not getting enough cardio this week. You could go out for a walk, or, you know—this is the kind of thing that makes sense.

Like, if you haven’t been sleeping enough, it could tell you what to do, suggest taking some vitamin D, right? Some iron, buying some protein powder. Chinese people are really lacking in things like protein and D3. Some of these things aren’t expensive if you just buy a little, and even a little can help.
But if they really did that, they’d become a niche product, and they wouldn’t be able to become...
For example, say everything is actually connected.

chapters.title: From smart-home readings to an assistant that works across devices

paragraphs.value: For example, going back to the smart home we were talking about: if you’re not sleeping well, what’s the core problem? It’s too dry and too hot. Who doesn’t have a temperature sensor or a humidifier or an air purifier at home? Couldn’t it just run automatically? It senses that something’s off. I’ve been using a whole Xiaomi smart-home setup lately. Sleep matters a lot to me because my nose feels terrible. I can’t handle being too hot or too cold, too dry or too humid. It’s really annoying.

I have both a humidifier and an air purifier, and I’ve put a humidity and temperature gauge in three places around the house. You find that Xiaomi’s own setup is just dumb. How dumb? Its humidifier only pays attention to its own sensor. Of course the humidity is highest right there—you’ve just sprayed water out of it.

It even tells me, “Humidity is holding steady at 50%.” In the next room, the humidifier is on, and the humidity gauge tells me it’s only 25%. This is exactly the kind of thing an agent should be handling. Because everything is connected. For example, if you didn’t sleep well, and in the morning you’re picking up or dropping off the kids, or thinking about what you need to do today, it could come up with some new things for you.

Set things up for you, or give you some new suggestions to help you get things done, or tell you to take a break, that kind of thing. Or say, “Maybe skip strength training today. You slept really badly, so don’t work out.” Or do a little less. Doesn’t Apple have this feature? But that readiness thing, right? That readiness thing… though it has pretty limited information.

Yeah, what I meant by what I just said was that all of these things are just entry points. Once you have an entry point, every agent is actually general-purpose. There’s a lot you can build out from there. What matters is establishing—one is the habit, and the other is trust in it.
Trust.

Look, from this angle, if you think back, you’ll see that what Ant Group has put out, including Lingguang and Afu, really does take a different path from those other companies. It’s been different all along. They haven’t piled on technology or work features; they’ve consistently started from the human side… from everyday life, more or less. They’ve kept driving things from that angle. I think that’s pretty good too.

Yeah.

For example, say we agree on a place to go together. Before, I’d have to start a group chat and @ each of you, and if I @ you too much, you get annoyed, right? That kind of thing. chapters.title: Why personal agents lag in China: constrained model responses and mobile-internet habits

paragraphs.value: Going back to the Personal Agent topic, China hasn’t kept up enough, has it? Could there be another reason? If you build a Personal Agent in China, you have to use a model that complies with Chinese regulations. Could those models just not be up to it either?

No, they can’t do it. Didn’t I say? We finished evaluating them. Not one domestic model can cut it. They can’t talk like a person the way Muse or Grok Bot can. So they can only deliver things in the form of coding and office work.
So that fits too, because if you’re serving users in China, you have to provide a model that complies with Chinese regulations.
The key thing is, they haven’t trained their models. They haven’t trained the latest models either.
You can do something like WorkBuddy, right? But the models aren’t good enough yet for a Personal Agent.

People still don’t agree on Personal Agents in China. They’re still questioning the whole thing, apart from Ant Group. People keep doubting its future. Even if, say, you don’t do things like business travel in China, there are still lots of opportunities.
We said last time that this generation of mobile internet was so strong that it created path dependence.

So at the beginning of the year, I told everyone to forget what you learned from the mobile internet. Even if you start building some web stuff today, building for the web isn't that hard, right? You can absolutely do it.
Look at us. If you've got a decent model, is it hard to write something? What are all those surplus engineers of yours doing?

Look at our website. This podcast is already one of the best among all these podcast websites out there. It's got all kinds of features, including our hyperlinks and links to friends' sites. Everyone, come join us. All of that is really simple to do.
Right, Qiaomu made this, and it can do editing now too, right? Editing is already live.

chapters.title: Give employees tokens and ownership: internal startups without large teams and resources

paragraphs.value: What Qiaomu just said suddenly gave me an idea. Don’t we want people to start businesses? It doesn’t actually cost anything. Just give them more tokens than their salary, allocate some tokens to each team, and let them build a product and be responsible for its profits and losses. Anyone can do it. You and I—we don’t promote it for you either. Go post about it on social media yourself. Isn’t that what we all do?

Who gives us money for anything, or how are we supposed to do it, right? You're already getting paid, right? I'm not giving you money for promotion either. Promote it yourself. If you can get it off the ground, then I'll give you...
You mean internal startups at Tencent.

That goes for any company, because things have matured now. In the past, internal startups weren’t mature; every time, they had to pour resources into them, arrange a bunch of PR and promotion, and so on. Now you can do it with three people.

I really have to emphasize this: I don't think people should go to work now and think of it as just showing up to work for the company. You have these incredibly powerful tools; you can absolutely go and build something. You can share in the returns from it together with the company.
Right.

The company would welcome it. If all you mean is, “The company assigns me a task, so I’ll finish it in half an hour and be done”—or even, “I’ll finish it in an hour, then spend the remaining seven hours slacking off and watching Red Fruit”—that mindset does you no good.
The company as an organization has to change in this era. It absolutely has to change.
Before, you kept saying—before, when it wasn't the right time, we kept talking about internal startups,
We shouldn’t have done internal startups, and yet we did.
When it was time to do internal startups, no one let you do them anymore. They don’t even release Personal Agent.
Yeah.
Right? So it's pretty strange.
